Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure and alert you to potential hypertension issues. However, they do not provide actual blood pressure readings.

Several smart rings and other fitness devices can do this, but require periodic calibration with a traditional cuff-style blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to provide full blood pressure measurements without calibration, citing a trial involving thousands of people to support this claim...

"The silent killer"

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and low blood pressure (hypotension) can both pose significant health risks.

Of the two, hypertension is more dangerous, known as the "silent killer," because it can cause severe and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart, and brain without obvious symptoms. This condition often only becomes apparent after triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Especially for the elderly, it is a good idea to measure blood pressure regularly, and home cuff-style blood pressure monitors are available on the market for self-measurement. However, the ideal scenario is fully automated monitoring through a fitness device you already wear.

Apple Watch's blood pressure feature

The launch of watchOS 26 enables five Apple Watch models to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these devices will not give you any readings, but will issue an alert when signs of possible hypertension are detected. Other devices such as the Oura Ring operate in a similar way.

Some fitness devices can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but require periodic calibration with readings from a cuff-style blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals claims to have successfully developed a smart ring that can achieve blood pressure measurements as accurate as traditional upper-arm cuff monitors without calibration—this is the Signal Ring.

According to Bloomberg, the company's CEO Tom Moss said he nearly died from undiagnosed hypertension, which motivated him to found the company.

The ring will begin pre-orders later today, with shipping in October, priced at US$399, with no subscription required. Real-time blood pressure readings and long-term tracking data will be displayed in the companion app (see image above).

It is worth noting that the Signal Ring is not currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that it measures accurate blood pressure readings on thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss does not intend to sell this ring to everyone—he says these professional features are most suitable for the elderly and those who have been told by a doctor that they are at risk for hypertension, implying that the Signal Ring may not be particularly outstanding in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
